title: When Ants Stare
subtitle: What Stares Back
editorial_note: This is an opening excerpt from a working draft. Obvious duplicated letters, stray editing marks, capitalization and punctuation have been lightly cleaned for this preview. The story and its unresolved questions are preserved.
paragraphs: It was morning, not early enough to be asleep, but not late enough to be considered normal. Like that period of time between dawn and dusk when you wake up—haphazardly even—to check if you’re late to class or you forgot to put on your alarm.
“We are having an open discussion this morning now. I know it’s early but we have something that happened recently that we should…”
“Sir, are you talking about the sun?”
Someone in the back, I don’t quite remember what their name was. I was too busy keeping my eyes open. Yesterday or… was it a month ago? I couldn’t really remember, and I guess I was the only one.
“Is there any comment from the government yet?”

Then I started to remember, half asleep in my own world. It started looking more like staring. Gazing into us. And then nothing. Back to normal, like it never happened. In a blink of an eye, the sun stared at the earth.
“No, there is no official news from the government.”
Silence, maybe the first time this class was actually quiet. Too quiet—but only for a second.
“We know nothing, so I wanted to ask a question to the class.”

It was rare for Mr. M to ask us something, especially this early and with a look as if we should answer honestly: “Do any of you have a good idea of what playing god is? What I mean by that is, when creating or using something turns from one extreme to another.”
“Wouldn’t the act change the outcome, like what is done with the information or things gained?”
“Yes, Miss Bright, it would all depend on the actions and thoughts of the individual.”

It was interesting, to say the least, as I looked up at the board and felt some sense of uncanny urgency to watch and listen—as I had no idea what was going to happen, or why, just that I should not LOOK AWAY.

“We humans,” he began to write, “have a sense of wonder to advance, for better or worse; we have time and time again played the part of the Fool, who understands nothing, yet without fail, works to understand.”
He finished his work on the whiteboard, full of different times in history and inventions.
“I’m just curious, when does something in the eyes of common people and those ahead of us or before us start to question the wisdom gained? Or are we so far gone to notice anymore?”
